lead: A staircase carries people between floors, and each sloping flight behaves as a slab bending along the slope. In the dog-legged form two flights run side by side in opposite directions, joined by a half landing at mid-height. The flight is designed as a simply supported one-way slab — the waist slab — spanning between landings, using the same flexure, shear and deflection checks as one-way slabs, plus one extra step: the sloping dead load is converted to load per metre of horizontal run.
prereq: You need: one-way slabs for the b d, Ast and shear routine, and cantilever and continuous slabs for support conditions at the landings.

sections.h3: Riser, tread, going and the dog-legged plan

blocks.text: The riser is the vertical height of one step; the tread its horizontal depth; the going is the tread without the nosing. A comfortable stair keeps 2 × riser + tread between 600 mm and 640 mm, so a 150 mm riser suits a 300 mm tread.

Number of risers = floor-to-floor height ÷ riser. A 3000 mm floor with 150 mm risers needs 20 risers, so 10 per flight and a 1500 mm rise per flight. In a dog-legged stair the two flights run parallel in opposite directions with a half landing at mid-height; there is no gap between the flights, so it fits a narrow rectangle. Most syllabi ask for this type.

items: Open well stair: a gap (well) between the flights, used where a lift or more light is wanted.
Straight flight: one long flight between floors; simple to design, needs a long plan.
Stringer beam stair: steps span between two sloping beams, so the steps carry the load, not a waist slab.
Spiral and cantilever tread stairs: treads cantilever from a central column or a wall; only a few universities teach these in detail.

sections.h3: The flight as a sloping one-way slab

blocks.text: The waist slab has thickness t measured perpendicular to the slope. Its weight per metre of horizontal run exceeds 25 t, because the slab is longer than its horizontal span. That correction is the slope factor:

blocks.where: R is the riser in mm, T the tread in mm. For R = 150 mm and T = 300 mm it is √(1 + 0.25) = 1.118.

blocks.text: Loads per metre width on the horizontal run: waist slab 25 t × slope factor; steps as a triangle, 25 × R/2 (R in metres); finish × slope factor; live load as given on plan. The effective span l is the horizontal distance between landing supports: clear span + d or centre-to-centre, whichever is smaller. Then Mu = wu l²/8 and V = wu l/2.

items: Fix riser, tread, number of risers and flight rise; compute the slope factor.
Take a 1 m strip, compute wu per metre of horizontal run, and Mu = wu l²/8.
d = t − cover − half the bar diameter; find Mu/(bd²) and pt; Ast = pt b d/100.
Check minimum steel 0.12% of b t for Fe415 (0.15% for Fe250); spacing ≤ 3d or 300 mm.
Shear: τv = V/(bd) ≤ k τc; a slab this deep needs no stirrups.
Distribution steel 0.12% of gross area across the slope, 8 mm bars.

blocks.text: The landing slab is designed separately as a short-span one-way slab spanning transversely between the floor beams or walls. Main flight bars run along the slope and are anchored into the landing; distribution bars run across. Cover 20 mm.

figure.caption: The two flights are inclined slabs spanning between the landings, and each landing slab spans across, the short way, between the floor beams.

spec.aria: A stair stack from top: flight 2 waist slab, landing slab, flight 1 waist slab with the slope factor 1.118, and floor beams carrying the reactions.

examples.question: Design the waist slab of a dog-legged staircase. Floor-to-floor height 3.0 m, riser 150 mm, tread 300 mm, so 10 risers per flight. Waist slab 150 mm thick, landing 1.2 m wide, effective span of each flight 3.3 m, live load 3.0 kN/m², floor finish 1.0 kN/m², M25 concrete, Fe415 steel, cover 20 mm.
steps: Rise per flight = 10 × 0.150 = 1.5 m. Slope factor = √(1 + (150/300)²) = 1.118.
Loads per metre of horizontal run: waist slab 25 × 0.150 × 1.118 = 4.19 kN/m; steps 25 × 0.150/2 = 1.88 kN/m; finish 1.0 × 1.118 = 1.12 kN/m; live 3.00 kN/m. Total w = 10.19 kN/m.
12 mm bars at 220 mm give 113.1 × 1000/220 = 514 mm² > 498 mm². Minimum 0.12% of 1000 × 150 = 180 mm², satisfied.
V = 15.28 × 3.3/2 = 25.2 kN. τv = 25.2 × 10³/(1000 × 124) = 0.203 N/mm², less than τc ≈ 0.44 N/mm² for pt = 0.40 and M25; with k = 1.30 for a 150 mm slab, k τc ≈ 0.57 N/mm². Safe.
Deflection: span/d = 3300/124 = 26.6 < 20 × 1.6 = 32 with the modification factor for pt ≈ 0.40 and fs ≈ 233 N/mm². Safe.
Distribution steel = 0.0012 × 1000 × 150 = 180 mm². Use 8 mm at 250 mm (201 mm²).
examples.answer: Provide a 150 mm waist slab with 12 mm main bars at 220 mm along the slope and 8 mm distribution bars at 250 mm across, for Mu = 20.80 kN·m and Ast = 498 mm².
examples.check:
sf = (1 + (150/300)**2)**0.5
w = 25*0.150*sf + 25*0.150/2 + 1.0*sf + 3.0
wu = 1.5*w
l = 3.3
M = wu*l*l/8
d = 150 - 20 - 6
m = M*1e6/(1000*d*d)
pt = 50*(1 - (1 - 4.598*M*1e6/(25*1000*d*d))**0.5)*25/415
Ast = pt*1000*d/100
V = wu*l/2
tv = V*1e3/(1000*d)
sd = l*1000/d
print(round(w,2))
print(round(wu,2))
print(round(M,2))
print(round(d,0))
print(round(m,3))
print(round(pt,3))
print(round(Ast,0))
print(round(V,1))
print(round(tv,3))
print(round(sd,1))

traps: Forgetting the slope factor understates the waist slab weight by about 12% for a 150/300 stair.

Using the sloping length (about 3.7 m in the example, i.e. 3.3 × 1.118) as the effective span instead of the horizontal distance between supports. The extra length is only for bar cutting and anchorage.
Applying the slope factor to the live load. Live load is specified on plan area, so it is used as it is; the factor applies only to the sloping waist slab and finishes.
Taking the step load as 25 × R per metre instead of 25 × R/2. The steps form a triangle over the horizontal run, not a rectangle.
Designing the landing slab as a continuation of the flight. It is a separate short-span slab spanning transversely between the floor beams.

quiz.a: Riser is the vertical rise of one step, tread its horizontal depth, going the tread measured without the nosing.

quiz.q: Why is a slope factor needed for the waist slab weight?
quiz.a: The thickness is measured perpendicular to the slope, so one metre of horizontal run contains more than one metre of slab; its weight per horizontal metre rises by √(1 + (R/T)²).

quiz.q: A stair has riser 160 mm and tread 280 mm. Find the slope factor.
Floor-to-floor height is 3.2 m with 160 mm risers in a dog-legged stair. How many risers per flight?
quiz.a: 3200/160 = 20 risers total, so 10 risers per flight, each flight rising 1.6 m.

quiz.q: A designer takes the flight span as the sloping length 3.7 m instead of the 3.3 m horizontal distance. What is the effect on the steel?
quiz.a: Moment rises in the ratio (3.7/3.3)² = 1.26; steel is about 26% heavier than needed, and shear is also overstated. Correct design uses the horizontal span.

quiz.q: Why is the landing slab designed separately from the flight?
quiz.a: It spans transversely between the floor beams or walls over the stair width, a different span and support condition from the inclined flight, and it also carries the flight reactions.

beyond: Not for the exam. Software models the flight as an inclined shell element, capturing the axial force in the waist slab that hand calculations ignore. Precast and steel stairs follow separate design codes, and fire escape stairs need a check on the loaded stair during evacuation. The same slope-factor logic appears in ramps and inclined roof slabs.
